19987-chapters-from-my-autobiography:
Mark Twain dictated his Chapters from My Autobiography late in life. He mocks the usual autobiographer in these pages. Conventional memoirists hunt out occasions that flatter them, he observes. In such scenes the author sees his own life reflected in print. Twain instead lets memory wander where it pleases. The chapters ran in the North American Review in 1906 and 1907. They were pieces of a vast dictated life he ordered sealed for a century.

Twain's method was talk: digressive, funny, and suddenly grave. He ranges from boyhood to fame without chronology's permission. The embargo made these chapters feel like messages in a bottle. Much was cut for contemporary feelings, on his design. What remains is the great voice thinking aloud. It is autobiography as performance, vintage Twain.
20007-lord-george-bentinck-a-political-b:
Disraeli wrote Lord George Bentinck as a political biography in 1852. Bentinck had led the Protectionist revolt against Sir Robert Peel. His sudden death in 1848 cut that leadership short. Disraeli recalls how Parliament congratulated itself on Bentinck's devotion. In an instant he was taken from them, he writes. Memory of the past and hope shaped that grief. The biography doubles as Disraeli's own defense.

Bentinck and Disraeli destroyed Peel over the Corn Laws together. The book argues their revolt was principle, not ambition. Racing, Bentinck's other life, gets its chapters too. Disraeli's portrait is warm, partisan, and brilliantly written. Political biography rarely admits its author so fully. This one is half its subject, half Disraeli.
20500-a-short-history-of-greek-philosoph:
A Short History of Greek Philosophy traces Greek thought from its first stirrings to its great schools. It starts with Thales and the thinkers of Ionia. For centuries before the Persian invasions, the book explains, Miletus led the Greek world.

Miletus stood near the centre of the Ionian coasts of Asia Minor. It was perhaps the greatest and wealthiest city of the Greek world, with four fine harbors. From such trading cities came the first questions about nature and the stuff of the world. The history follows those questions through Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle in plain order.
20626-torchy:
Sewell Ford's Torchy, published in 1909, introduces the red-headed office boy whose slangy narration made the series famous. Torchy works the door and the buzzer of a big New York trust company. He tells his own story in the street talk of the day.

This time, Torchy says, he got a bug that the new Octopus Building might have been put up special for him. Anyway, it looked good from the outside, and he blows in through the plate-glass merry-go-round. The arcade is all to the butterscotch, with everything handy. Ford's Torchy stories ran for years in magazines and books.
21624-fifteen-chapters-of-autobiography:
George W. E. Russell, a Liberal politician and writer, tells his own life in Fifteen Chapters of Autobiography. The book first appeared as One Look Back, and Nelson issued this edition. It opens at a wooden temple in Lincoln's Inn Fields, over the spot where his ancestor Lord Russell was beheaded.

Chapters run from beginnings through Harrow and Oxford to London and hospitality. Electioneering, Parliament, politics, and oratory fill the middle of the tale. Literature and service close a life spent near the centre of Victorian public life. Russell writes with warmth and a rich store of anecdotes about the great folk he knew.
21759-kate-coventry-an-autobiography:
Kate Coventry tells her own story in this novel, presented as an autobiography and edited by G. J. Whyte-Melville. It opens on a rainy June morning in London, with Kate fighting tears over a spoiled trip to Ascot. She had ordered a peach-colored mantle and a fine new bonnet for Cup Day. Her Aunt Deborah thinks the outing should be given up.

Kate is quick, frank, and unlike most girls of her circle, or so her aunt says. The tale follows her through family, society, and the excitements of a young woman's season. Horses and the hunting world, Whyte-Melville's own ground, run through her story. Her voice, bright and unbothered, carries the book from the first page.
21882-the-house-of-torchy:
Torchy, the wisecracking New York office boy grown up, takes a wife in Sewell Ford's The House of Torchy, published in 1917. The opening finds Torchy and Vee on a sleigh ride to a hotel register, marriage on his mind. Getting married, he says, is the biggest sporting chance he ever took. The chapters then follow the pair through jobs, friends, and wartime turns.

Vee goes over the top, Torchy gets the call, and the house of Torchy is founded at last. Ford tells it all in Torchy's slang, a Broadway patter that made the series a favorite. Arthur William Brown drew the pictures. It is light American humor of the teens, fast, kind, and full of city talk.
22204-the-making-of-a-novelist-an-experi:
David Christie Murray subtitled The Making of a Novelist an experiment in autobiography. A book in a shop window starts the experiment. Seeing it in Lipscombe's window made Murray younger by twenty years in a minute. A rush of recollections followed, and he resolved then and there to put his memories on paper.

He traces his path from a Midlands childhood to a London career in letters. Apprenticeship, journalism, failure, and success all get honest chapters. Murray asks what makes a novelist: gift, hunger, luck, or grind. The book answers from one life, told plainly. It remains a handy source on the professional writer's world in Victorian England.
22911-where-we-live-a-home-geography:
Emilie V. Jacobs teaches geography from the schoolhouse door in Where We Live, a home geography for young pupils. Her questions start with the building itself. How many kinds of workers did our schoolhouse need before it could rise? Who supplied its stone and slate? Where did its iron, steel, tin, and timber come from?

Lessons grow outward from those familiar things, to town, state, and wider world. The method trusts children to reason from what they can touch. Each answer reveals a chain of workers and materials behind ordinary objects. Books of this kind shaped how American children first pictured their country. Jacobs's version stands out for its patience and its respect for a child's own street.
a-mortal-antipathy: Oliver Wendell Holmes's 1885 A Mortal Antipathy: a young man's strange aversion, cured by love. The doctor's last novel, gentle and wise. A pleasant romance of healing. Holmes's last novel cures aversion with love, gentle and wise.
a-new-philosophy: Édouard Le Roy's early-1900s work of philosophy, associated with Bergson's circle, on intuition, science, and the nature of thought. Dense but suggestive, it represents the French "new philosophy" that challenged cold rationalism. For students of modern thought, a significant document.
beautiful-joe-an-autobiography: Marshall Saunders's 1893 Beautiful Joe: a dog's autobiography, the Black Beauty of canines. The true story that moved the world. The classic humane tale. Joe's sufferings taught kindness to millions, the dog book that changed laws.
black-hawk-autobiography:
Black Hawk, the Sauk war leader, dictated his autobiography in 1833 through an interpreter. It was the first Native American autobiography published in English. Black Hawk was then a prisoner after the war that bears his name.

He tells of his youth, his wars, and the treaties that stripped the Sauk of their lands. The disputed 1804 treaty, he argues, was never fairly made or understood by his people. His account of the 1832 war gives the conflict from the Native side. Sorrow and defiance run through the whole story, told in his own cadence. An editor named Patterson helped shape the spoken words for print.
carnegie-autobiography:
Andrew Carnegie wrote his autobiography late in life, and it appeared in 1920, a year after his death. The Scottish immigrant had risen from bobbin boy to steel king. Then he gave his fortune away to libraries and learning.

He tells of his poor Dunfermline childhood, the crossing to America, and work as a telegraph boy in Pittsburgh. Railroads, iron, and finally steel built his empire, step by shrewd step. His Gospel of Wealth teaching, that the rich must give back, shapes the later chapters. The book is both a business story and a case for philanthropy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrosian-hym: A 1913 entry on Ambrosian hymnography — the hymns of St. Ambrose and his school. Hugh Henry unfolds their stately stanzas. Veni Redemptor gentium leads the choir. The Church sings them still. The father of Latin hymnody. Their meter is the stately iambic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anarchy: This 1913 reference piece on anarchy — the creed of no-rule. Thomas Campbell judges it in Catholic morals. Order is nature's own law. The Church condemns the chaos. A philosophy of the wrecking ball. Its bombs shook the nineteenth century. Its creed denies all authority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-de-mo: A 1913 entry on Antoine de Mouchy — the inquisitor of the Huguenots. Leo Kelly tells his stern part. His Demochares scourged the heretics. The Sorbonne backed his zeal. The hammer of the French reformers. His name was the Huguenots' terror. His tomb lies in Parisian soil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arabian-schoo: A 1913 entry on the Arabian school of philosophy — Averroes and his kin. William Turner weighs their Aristotelian lore. Their commentaries schooled the West. St. Thomas answered their errors. The philosophers of Cordoba and Baghdad. Their logic shaped the medieval schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustin-loui: A 1913 entry on Augustin-Louis Cauchy — the prince of mathematicians. Henry Brock honors his seven hundred memoirs. His analysis remade the science. His charity matched his genius. A saint among the geometers. His name marks the Paris streets. His theorems fill the textbooks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-austro-hungar: This 1913 reference article on the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy — the dual empire's church story. Cölestin Wolfsgrüber tells its Catholic past. The emperor bore the apostolic crown. The nations strained the old bond. The empire of the Danube's faith. Its concordat shaped the imperial church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baconian-syst: A 1913 entry on the Baconian system of philosophy — Francis Bacon's new organon. Francis Aveling weighs its famous method. Induction would conquer nature's secrets. The Church sifted its proud claims. The herald of the experimental age. His idols warned the careless thinker.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomew-m: A 1913 entry on Bartholomew MacCarthy — an Irish scholar of note. John MacErlean records his works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the Gaelic studies. A scholar of the Irish past. His annals serve the Celtic scholars. His work aids the annalists still.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biblical-geog: A 1913 entry on biblical geography — the lands of the sacred story. Charles Souvay maps the holy places. The hills and valleys frame the text. The pilgrim walks the ancient roads. The atlas of the Bible. Its maps mark the patriarchs' journeys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-ico: This 1913 reference piece on Christian iconography — the language of the sacred image. The entry deciphers its hallowed signs. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cynic-school-: A 1913 entry on the Cynic school — the tub-dwelling philosophers. William Turner unfolds their austere creed. Diogenes scorned the world's goods. The barrel was the sage's home. The beggars of the ancient wisdom. Their Antisthenes was the founder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cyrenaic-scho: This 1913 reference piece on the Cyrenaic school — the pleasure's philosophers. William Turner unfolds their gay creed. Aristippus crowned the present joy. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dennis-floren: This 1913 reference piece on Dennis Florence MacCarthy — the Irish poet. Thomas Kennedy honors his famous translations. His pen rendered Calderón's verse. The nation prized its gentle bard. The singer of the Irish muse. His Bell-founder is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eparchy: A 1913 entry on the eparchy — the Eastern diocese. Adrian Fortescue unfolds its Greek form. The bishop rules the eparchial flock. The patriarch guards the ancient bounds. The diocese of the Eastern Church. Its exarch is the bishop's peer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hagiography: A 1913 entry on hagiography — the saints' writing. Hippolyte Delehaye unfolds the learned art. The Bollandists sift the pious tales. The scholars weigh the ancient Lives. The science of the saintly legends. Its Bollandist method is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heptarchy: A 1913 entry on the Heptarchy — the seven kingdoms. Herbert Thurston unfolds the Saxon tale. The Angles ruled the island's realms. The monks lit the pagan dark. The kingdoms of the early England. Its 5th-century realms are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hierarchy: A 1913 entry on hierarchy — the sacred order. Alphonse Van Hove unfolds its classic degrees. The pope crowns the episcopal rank. The priests serve the holy altars. The ranks of the Catholic ministry. Its three orders are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ionian-school: This 1913 reference piece on the Ionian school — the nature philosophers. William Turner unfolds their ancient lore. Thales sought the primal stuff. The sages weighed the seemly cause. The fathers of the Greek science. Its 6th-century sages are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-mullanph: A 1913 entry on Mullanphy — the St. Louis philanthropist. Thomas Meehan honors his famous charities. His gold built the western Church. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-justin-mccart: This 1913 reference piece on McCarthy — the Irish historian. Andrew MacErlean honors his famous History. His pen chronicled the nation's past. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neo-pythagore: The Neo-Pythagoreans revived Pythagoras's number-mysticism in the Roman Empire, blending mathematics with religious aspiration. This entry covers their doctrines, their sages, and their influence. Philosophy as a way of salvation: their sage Apollonius rivaled Christ in pagan legend and literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-tuit: This biographical entry profiles Nicholas Tuite MacCarthy, an Irish Jesuit preacher of the 1800s, tracing his career, his celebrated sermons, and his place among the orators of his age as the 1913 editors recorded it. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palaeography: Palaeography is the science of ancient handwriting, the key that unlocks the manuscripts. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-gandolp: This biographical entry profiles Peter Gandolphy, an English Jesuit preacher of the 1800s, tracing his career, his sermons, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philosophy: Philosophy is the love of wisdom, and this great entry surveys its history from Thales to the moderns. The 1913 editors' masterful conspectus of the whole discipline. The queen of the sciences: its long history spans twenty-five crowded centuries of thought.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piauhy: Piauhy, the Brazilian state of the dry northeast, became a diocese serving its scattered faithful. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history as of 1913. The faith in the land of the sertão: its lonely missions brave the drought.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reorganizatio: The reorganization of the English hierarchy was Pius IX's act of 1850. This entry traces its causes, its dioceses, and its storms. The restoration of the sees: its papal bull woke the nation in 1850's autumn of anger and fear.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-semitic-epigr: Semitic epigraphy is the science of the ancient inscriptions. This entry examines its finds, its scripts, and its Bible light. The stones of the Semitic past: their carved scripts guard the Bible in the 1800s' scholars in the academies of the West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-malachy: St. Malachy was the archbishop of Armagh. This entry traces his Clairvaux, his reform, and his fame. The prophet of the Irish church: his great see crowned Armagh in the 1130s' Ulster in the north of the province in the Navan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stoics-and-st: The Stoics were the philosophers of the Porch. This long entry examines their Zeno, their virtue, and their influence. The sages of the Roman empire: their painted Porch crowned Athens in the 300s BC of the Stoa in the Agora.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-telepathy: Telepathy is the question of mind reading. This entry traces its psychology and its evidence. The alleged commerce of distant minds: its strange claims filled the journals in the 1880s' London in the society of the truly very old researchers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theosophy: Theosophy is the wisdom of the divine. This long entry examines its Blavatsky, its doctrines, and its history. The doctrine of the hidden masters: its fateful 1875 crowned New York in the society of the Blavatsky in the old hall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-o-herl: O'Herlahy was the bishop of Ross. This entry traces his 1500s, his persecution, and his death. The martyr of the Irish church: his lonely Ross crowned Cork in the 1560s of the persecution in the truly very old green hills.
coolidge-autobiography:
Calvin Coolidge published his autobiography in 1929, just after leaving the White House. True to his nickname, Silent Cal keeps the style spare and plain. He traces his rise from a Vermont farm to the presidency.

Coolidge recalls his father's store, his law practice, and his climb through Massachusetts politics. He became president on Warren Harding's sudden death in 1923, then won his own term. The Roaring Twenties appear here without noise or boast. Readers value the book for its calm voice and its glimpse of a frugal, vanished New England. He gives his early years more space than his time in the White House.
doe-osti-17038167-gas-phase-chemical-phy: Hypersonic chemistry got its DOE physics report, and this text covers gas-phase chemical physics in extreme environments. The pages detail the reactions at Mach speed. The aerospace chemists get their data. The physics was extreme. The data were hypersonic.

essays-in-librarianship-and-bibliography: Essays in Librarianship and Bibliography, Richard Garnett's essays. The librarian's craft. This book preserves that work. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
franklin-autobiography:
Benjamin Franklin began writing his autobiography in 1771, meaning it as a letter to his son. He worked on it in bursts over nearly twenty years, and it stayed unfinished at his death in 1790. No American life story has been copied more often.

Franklin tells of his Boston childhood, his runaway start as a printer, and his rise in Philadelphia. He lists his plan for moral perfection, thirteen virtues tracked in a little notebook. Work, thrift, and self-teaching carry him from rags to fame. The book became the pattern of the American self-made life, read by schoolchildren and statesmen alike.
ignatius-autobiography:
Ignatius of Loyola dictated his autobiography in the 1550s, near the end of his life, at his companions' urging. He speaks of himself in the third person, as 'the pilgrim.' The short work tells how a vain soldier became a saint and founder.

A cannonball shattered his leg at Pamplona in 1521, and during his slow healing he turned to Christ and the saints. Pilgrimage, poverty, study in Paris, and the founding of the Jesuits follow. Ignatius is frank about his pride, his tears, and his visions. The text remains a key source for his life and the order he built.
is-shakespeare-dead-from-my-autobiograph: Mark Twain argues, with his best riverboat humor, that Bacon and not the Stratford man wrote the plays. Right or wrong, the ride is hilarious. The great American skeptic takes on the greatest English question, and the fun never stops.
james-nasmyth-engineer-an-autobiography: James Nasmyth's autobiography: the inventor of the steam hammer tells his own story. Modest, ingenious, and full of Victorian engineering, it is a classic of industrial life. The self-made engineer at his best. Nasmyth's hammer built the iron age, and his book built his fame.
man-and-superman-a-comedy-and-a-philosop:
Man and Superman is Bernard Shaw's comedy and philosophy in play form. His dedicatory letter answers the critic Arthur Bingham Walkley. Walkley had once asked him why he never wrote a Don Juan play. Shaw replies that the day of reckoning has arrived at last.

He warns Walkley that the play's morals are his to justify. Its hero is a modern Don Juan, hunted rather than hunting. The famous Don Juan in Hell scene debates life in dream form. Shaw turns courtship upside down with wit and paradox. Ann, the heroine, pursues her man in the name of Life. The play stands among Shaw's greatest and gayest works.
mark-twain-s-burlesque-autobiography:
Mark Twain's Burlesque Autobiography appeared in 1871 with his 'First Romance.' Two or three persons, he says, begged for his life story. He yields at last to this frenzied public demand. His is a noble old house, stretching far into antiquity.

The earliest Twain ancestor on record was a friend named Higgins. That was in the eleventh century, in Aberdeen, county of Cork, England. Why the line bears the mother's name remains a family mystery. So runs the joke, through a pedigree of pure nonsense. The companion piece burlesques awful, terrible medieval romance. It is early Twain, playful and already unmistakable.
mr-dooley-s-philosophy:
Finley Peter Dunne's Mr. Dooley discourses here on the year's passing show, illustrated by F. Opper. The dedication reads: to the Hennessys of the world who suffer and are silent. Dunne's preface calls Dooley a great and learned man, with mock solemnity. Most papers appeared first in the American and English press.

The contents tour the headlines: the Transvaal War and the Boer mission. China, Minister Wu, and the yacht races follow. Servant girls, polygamy, Kentucky politics, and young oratory all receive judgments. Dooley, an Irish bartender in Chicago, explains the world to his friend Hennessy in dialect that hides sharp political sense.
nasa-tm-19670030170-clean-rooms-a-select:
The Kennedy Space Center Library at NASA's Florida spaceport compiled this reading list in September 1967. Its subject is clean rooms, the near-dustless rooms where spacecraft are assembled and prepared. The introduction explains that the drive for the most sterile conditions in space flight had produced a vast technical literature on the subject.

An earlier Kennedy bibliography on clean rooms, issued in December 1965 by Tena Crenshaw and Mary Kihm, listed the library's holdings. Continued interest in contamination control led to this expanded reissue, prepared by Ruth Perks. Entries are organized into five groups: journal articles first, then documents, meeting symposia, books, and finally specifications and standards. The catalog record adds keeping spacecraft clean as the list's wider theme, and the compiler invites comments on its usefulness.
nasa-tm-19680022619-management-a-selecti:
Management: A Selective Bibliography was compiled by the Kennedy Space Center Library and approved by R. A. Lindemann, chief of its Historical and Library branch. Running the Moon program demanded strong managers as much as strong engineers. The bibliography answers a question the library heard often: what books should a manager read?

Entries run in title order, with author and subject indexes to help readers find material. The compiler annotated only books that could be examined firsthand, keeping the notes honest. Sample titles cover side fields, insurance among them. An appendix lists further reading in the management field, from contracts to cost control.
nasa-tm-19700011550-motivation-a-selecte:
Staff at the Kennedy Space Center Library prepared this selected bibliography, issued on February 20, 1970, as document GP-816. Its subject is motivation, the forces that move people to act, work, and keep trying. The entries lean toward management, since the readers in mind were managers and students of management.

Each entry gives full publishing details, a library call number, and a short note on what the book covers. The sample pages list works on handling weak job performance and on attitudes at work. Others treat managing young adults and using company records in marketing research. The notes often say plainly who should read a book and what use they would get from it.
nasa-tm-19720010765-apollo-13-lunar-phot:
The National Space Science Data Center at the Goddard Space Flight Center issued this Apollo 13 photographic data package in December 1970. Apollo 13 never landed after its oxygen tank explosion. Its crews still photographed the Moon and Earth during the free return flight. The package gives investigators complete information on that photography. It also helps them choose frames for review and study.

Three parts make up the package. A data users' note describes the mission's photo goals, gear, coverage, and quality. Frame indexes cover all seventy millimeter and sixteen millimeter pictures. A catalog section prints proof copies of the Earth and Moon frames. Ordering forms and index maps are enclosed. United States users ordered through the data center itself.
news-from-the-duchy:
A. T. Quiller-Couch, who signed himself Q, gathered News from the Duchy as tales from his Cornish duchy. He dedicated the book to his friend Austin M. Purves, of Philadelphia and Troy Town. Part one opens with Pipes in Arcady. Our Lady of Gwithian and Pilot Matthey's Christmas follow.

Other tales in part one name the Mont-Bazillac, three necklaces, and a wren. The Honour of the Ship, Lieutenant Lapenotiere, and The Cask Ashore keep the sea in view. Part two holds Ye Sexes, Give Ear and Frenchman's Creek. Sailors, pilots, and small town folk fill Q's pages, in a Cornwall he knew street by street.
on-with-torchy:
Sewell Ford wrote this comic novel about office boy Torchy. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York. Ford had written Torchy and Trying Out Torchy before. Foster Lincoln drew the pictures for this volume. Chapter one is called Chancing It for Vee.

Torchy pulls a sleuth stunt and bugs the office system. He shunts gloom for his boss in one chapter. Peggy, Gladys, and Bunny pass through his busy days. Torchy talks in lively New York slang throughout. Ford writes light tales of clerks, bosses, and sweethearts. The book suits readers who enjoy cheerful office comedy.
podcast-joerogan-Kv3dsPkTvhY:
Physicist Frank von Hippel joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1540 to talk about nuclear policy. Von Hippel worked in the White House and has spent his career on arms control and reactor safety. He brings an insider's memory to questions most people only meet in headlines.

He and Rogan discuss the state of the world's arsenals, the risk of accidents, and the hard choices inside civilian nuclear power. Rogan asks plain questions about worst cases and how close the world has come. The episode is a calm, expert briefing on the weapons that still shadow every other subject the show covers.
podcast-joerogan-X9JLij1obHY:
Eric Weinstein's episode 1203 of the Joe Rogan Experience is an early entry in his long run of visits. Weinstein, a mathematician and investor, was then introducing his grand physics theory and his critique of timid science to wide audiences. Rogan's studio became his loudest platform.

He argues that universities reward safe work and exile bold minds, and he sketches the unified theory he says he was discouraged from publishing. Rogan asks him to slow down and translate. The episode is the starting gun for one of the show's defining guest arcs, full of the confidence and grievance that mark all his later talks.
tacitus-dialogue-oratory-murphy:
Arthur Murphy translated Tacitus's Dialogue Concerning Oratory, a short debate on public speaking. Friends gather and ask why great oratory faded in Rome. Each speaker gives a rival answer in turn.

One blames soft schools and lazy youth for the decline. Another argues that peace under emperors killed the need for bold speech. A poet guest defends a quiet life of verse instead. The talk is graceful, witty, and short. It offers the talk of talk itself, from an age that prized fine speech as a high public art. Murphy's English keeps the talk light on its feet.
the-adventure-of-living-a-subjective-aut: John St. Loe Strachey, the influential editor of The Spectator, looks back on a life at the center of British journalism and public debate. He recalls the politicians, writers, and controversies he knew, all filtered through his own strong opinions. the-log-cabin-lady-an-anonymous-autobiog: Published anonymously through editor Marie Mattingly Meloney, this is the plain-spoken life story of a pioneer woman. the-story-of-my-heart-an-autobiography: Dying young, Richard Jefferies wrote this hymn to the life he felt pulsing in field and sky. It is less a memoir than a prayer to nature. Strange, burning, and beautiful: the testament of England's nature-mystic.
theodore-roosevelt-an-autobiography: Theodore Roosevelt's 1913 autobiography: the Rough Rider's own story. Ranch, war, and White House. The strenuous life in his words. An American classic, roosevelt's own strenuous life, ranch, war, White House, an American classic, 1913, the Rough Rider.
theodore-roosevelt-an-intimate-biography: William Roscoe Thayer's intimate biography of Theodore Roosevelt: the Rough Rider, president, and force of nature. Warm, admiring, and well-informed, it captures his vitality. The standard early life. Thayer knew Roosevelt, and his portrait is vivid.
trollope-autobiography:
Anthony Trollope wrote his autobiography in 1875 and 1876, but it appeared only in 1883, after his death. Trollope was among the most popular novelists of Victorian England. His frank account of the writing trade shocked readers who liked genius to seem effortless.

He tells of an unhappy schoolboy life, debt, and slow years as a postal clerk in Ireland. Then comes his famous method: 250 words every fifteen minutes, 2,500 before breakfast, watch on the desk. Trollope lists each novel and what it earned, to the pound. The book remains a classic portrait of writing as honest daily work.
